mcqs.q: The crucial constitutional shield against self-incrimination embedded in Article 20(3) is legally available to:

options.A: Any individual formally accused of an offence, encompassing both citizens and foreign nationals
options.B: Strictly Indian citizens, denying the protection to alien entities
options.C: Individuals facing prosecution strictly for severe cognizable offences carrying sentences exceeding seven years
options.D: Individuals exclusively during the formal trial phase, offering no protection during police interrogations

mcqs.q: Analyze the scope of the right to practice any profession or carry on any trade under Article 19(1)(g). Which of the following assertions is constitutionally valid?

options.A: The State possesses the explicit constitutional authority to create a partial or complete monopoly in any trade or business, excluding citizens from it.
options.B: The constitutional right is absolute, prohibiting the State from imposing technical or professional qualifications.
options.C: The right immunizes commercial businesses from state regulation, even if their operations conflict with public interest.
options.D: The State is completely barred from restricting commercial activities, including those inherently dangerous to public health.

mcqs.q: The Constitution does not explicitly define the term 'minority' as utilized in Article 30. Through judicial interpretation (notably in TMA Pai), the Supreme Court has established that minority status must be determined:

options.A: Strictly on the basis of the demographic population of the concerned individual State, not the entire nation
options.B: Exclusively at the macro national level, relying on pan-India census data
options.C: Solely on the basis of religious affiliation, rendering linguistic demographics irrelevant
options.D: Exclusively by parliamentary statute, precluding judicial intervention in demographic classification

mcqs.q: To prevent the State from bypassing fundamental rights by acting through corporate veils, the Supreme Court laid down the definitive six-point test to determine if a body is an 'instrumentality or agency of the State' under Article 12 in the landmark case of:

options.A: Ajay Hasia vs. Khalid Mujib Sehravardi
options.B: Sabhajit Tewary vs. Union of India
options.C: Naresh Shridhar Mirajkar vs. State of Maharashtra
options.D: Ujjambai vs. State of U.P.

mcqs.q: Demonstrating the dynamic nature of constitutional interpretation, the Supreme Court overruled its previous stance in Sabhajit Tewary, ultimately holding that the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) qualifies as 'State' under Article 12 in the case of:

options.A: Pradeep Kumar Biswas vs. Indian Institute of Chemical Biology
options.B: Zee Telefilms Ltd. vs. Union of India
options.C: R.D. Shetty vs. International Airport Authority
options.D: Sukhdev Singh vs. Bhagatram

mcqs.q: Regarding the complex constitutional status of the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) as adjudicated by the Supreme Court (Zee Telefilms case), which statement accurately reflects its position?

options.A: It is definitively classified as 'State' under Article 12, making it directly subject to writ petitions under Article 32.
options.B: It is not 'State' under Article 12; however, because it discharges vital public functions, it is amenable to the broader writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226.
options.C: It is recognized as a purely private, autonomous body entirely immune from both Article 32 and Article 226 scrutiny.
options.D: It is a statutory body explicitly created by an Act of Parliament and therefore implicitly bound by Part III.

mcqs.q: For a legislative classification to survive the rigorous scrutiny of Article 14, constitutional jurisprudence dictates it must cumulatively satisfy twin tests. These foundational tests are:

options.A: The classification must be founded on an 'intelligible differentia', and this differentia must possess a 'rational nexus' to the object sought to be achieved by the statute.
options.B: The classification must demonstrate mathematical exactness and strict geographical separation.
options.C: The law must be free of manifest arbitrariness and possess historical precedence in common law.
options.D: The legislation must strictly demonstrate absolute legislative competence and receive prior presidential assent.

mcqs.q: The doctrine of 'Manifest Arbitrariness' has evolved into a potent judicial weapon to strike down legislation under Article 14. This doctrine was pivotally utilized to invalidate laws in which of the following landmark cases?

options.A: Shayara Bano vs. Union of India (Invalidation of Triple Talaq)
options.B: Joseph Shine vs. Union of India (Decriminalization of Adultery)
options.C: Navtej Singh Johar vs. Union of India (Reading down of Section 377)
options.D: All of the above landmark judgments relied heavily on this doctrine

mcqs.q: In the foundational Romesh Thappar vs. State of Madras (1950) judgment, the Supreme Court struck down a state ban on the circulation of a magazine. The Court established a high threshold, ruling that freedom of speech could NOT be restricted merely for 'public order', but only for:

options.A: General disruption of localized public peace
options.B: Aggravated threats severely imperiling the 'Security of the State' or tending to overthrow it
options.C: Acts prejudicing friendly relations with foreign states
options.D: Statements amounting to criminal contempt of court

mcqs.q: The Supreme Court aggressively protected press freedom by striking down the Newsprint Control Order, which arbitrarily fixed the maximum page limit for newspapers, holding it an unconstitutional infringement of Article 19(1)(a) in:

options.A: Sakal Papers (P) Ltd. vs. Union of India
options.B: Bennett Coleman & Co. vs. Union of India
options.C: Express Newspapers vs. Union of India
options.D: Brij Bhushan vs. State of Delhi

mcqs.q: Citing its vague phrasing and massive 'chilling effect' on free speech in cyberspace, the Supreme Court declared Section 66A of the Information Technology Act entirely unconstitutional and violative of Article 19(1)(a) in the landmark case of:

options.A: Shreya Singhal vs. Union of India
options.B: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy vs. Union of India
options.C: Anuradha Bhasin vs. Union of India
options.D: PUCL vs. Union of India

mcqs.q: Expanding the protective ambit of free speech, the Supreme Court ruled that 'commercial speech' (including corporate advertisements) is a constitutionally protected derivative of Article 19(1)(a) in the case of:

options.A: Hamdard Dawakhana vs. Union of India
options.B: Tata Press Ltd. vs. MTNL
options.C: Indian Express Newspapers vs. Union of India
options.D: LIC vs. Manubhai D. Shah

mcqs.q: While upholding the constitutional validity of Section 124A of the IPC (Sedition), the Supreme Court strictly circumscribed its application, stating it applies ONLY to acts involving intention or tendency to create public disorder or incitement to violence. This defining standard was set in:

options.A: Kedar Nath Singh vs. State of Bihar
options.B: S.G. Vombatkere vs. Union of India
options.C: Balwant Singh vs. State of Punjab
options.D: Tara Singh Gopi Chand vs. State

mcqs.q: Adjudicating the legality of sweeping internet shutdowns in Jammu & Kashmir (Anuradha Bhasin vs. Union of India, 2020), the Supreme Court laid down that:

options.A: The fundamental right to access the internet is absolute, rendering any state-mandated suspension inherently unconstitutional.
options.B: Indefinite suspension of internet services is unconstitutional; any restriction must satisfy the rigorous test of proportionality and be subject to periodic review.
options.C: Internet suspension is purely an executive policy decision concerning national security, completely immunized from judicial review.
options.D: Access to high-speed (4G) internet is not a fundamental right, thereby allowing the State unfettered discretion to throttle bandwidth indefinitely.

mcqs.q: Which monumental judgment effectively buried the 'Mutual Exclusivity' theory propagated in A.K. Gopalan, establishing instead that Articles 14, 19, and 31 (then existing) are not isolated silos but form an interconnected, synthesized constitutional code?

options.A: R.C. Cooper vs. Union of India (The Bank Nationalisation Case)
options.B: Kesavananda Bharati vs. State of Kerala
options.C: Minerva Mills vs. Union of India
options.D: I.R. Coelho vs. State of Tamil Nadu

mcqs.q: Operating in a legislative vacuum, the Supreme Court in Vishaka vs. State of Rajasthan laid down binding guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace, observing that such harassment constitutes a direct violation of which specific Fundamental Rights?

options.A: Articles 14 (Equality), 15 (Non-discrimination), and 21 (Life and Liberty)
options.B: Strictly Articles 19 (Freedom of profession) and 25 (Freedom of religion)
options.C: Articles 23 (Prohibition of trafficking) and 24 (Prohibition of child labor)
options.D: Articles 15, 16 (Equality in employment), and 17 (Abolition of untouchability)

mcqs.q: In the complex adjudication of Olga Tellis vs. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985), while the Court famously recognized the 'right to livelihood', what was its ultimate procedural ruling regarding the eviction of pavement dwellers?

options.A: It ruled that pavement dwellers possess an absolute, non-derogable right to occupy public spaces for their livelihood.
options.B: Eviction was declared constitutionally valid only if the State first provided permanent alternative accommodation to every displaced individual.
options.C: It upheld the evictions but mandated that the procedure for eviction must be just, fair, and reasonable, incorporating the principles of natural justice (right to be heard).
options.D: It ruled that the State possesses the unbridled, arbitrary power to evict trespassers on public property without notice.

mcqs.q: The Supreme Court extensively analyzed the scope of preventive detention, the rights of the detenu, and upheld the overarching constitutional validity of the National Security Act (NSA) in the landmark judgment of:

options.A: A.K. Roy vs. Union of India
options.B: Sunil Batra vs. Delhi Administration
options.C: Babu Singh vs. State of U.P.
options.D: Charles Sobhraj vs. Superintendent, Central Jail

mcqs.q: To combat the systemic menace of custodial torture and deaths, the Supreme Court issued a comprehensive set of mandatory procedural guidelines to be adhered to by police personnel during arrest, detention, and interrogation in the case of:

options.A: D.K. Basu vs. State of West Bengal
options.B: Nilabati Behera vs. State of Orissa
options.C: Joginder Kumar vs. State of U.P.
options.D: Rudul Sah vs. State of Bihar

mcqs.q: Elevating the discourse on human rights, the Supreme Court explicitly declared that 'the right to life includes the right to live with human dignity and all that goes along with it', forcefully rejecting the notion that life is mere animal existence, in:

options.A: Francis Coralie Mullin vs. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi
options.B: Kharak Singh vs. State of U.P.
options.C: Unni Krishnan vs. State of A.P.
options.D: Prem Shankar Shukla vs. Delhi Administration

mcqs.q: The harrowing reality of undertrial prisoners languishing in jails led the Supreme Court to recognize the 'right to a speedy trial' as an implicit, unalienable guarantee flowing from Article 21 in the foundational case of:

options.A: Hussainara Khatoon vs. Home Secretary, State of Bihar
options.B: M.H. Hoskot vs. State of Maharashtra
options.C: Sheela Barse vs. State of Maharashtra
options.D: Khatri vs. State of Bihar

mcqs.q: Prioritizing human life over bureaucratic procedure, the Supreme Court held that every medical practitioner, across government and private sectors, has a binding professional obligation to provide immediate assistance in medico-legal cases without awaiting police formalities. This paradigm shift occurred in:

options.A: Parmanand Katara vs. Union of India
options.B: Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity vs. State of West Bengal
options.C: Consumer Education & Research Centre vs. Union of India
options.D: Vincent Panikurlangara vs. Union of India

mcqs.q: Reinforcing the integrity of the criminal justice system, the Supreme Court emphasized that Article 21 encompasses the right to a 'fair trial', detailing that this requires an unbiased judge, a competent prosecutor, and an atmosphere totally free from intimidation, in the Best Bakery case officially known as:

options.A: Zahira Habibullah Sheikh vs. State of Gujarat
options.B: Sushila Aggarwal vs. State (NCT of Delhi)
options.C: Siddhartha Vashisht @ Manu Sharma vs. State (NCT of Delhi)
options.D: Mohd. Ajmal Amir Kasab vs. State of Maharashtra
